text.en: The Chazon Ish's parable: what matters is not holding one's old post but standing where the battle is now, so if children understand Ivrit they must be taught in it.
The small kaf in Avraham's weeping means that Sarah did not truly die for him: separated in body, they remain united in soul.
Sarah's levayah, the first in the Torah, is placed before the first shidduch in the Torah to teach what a Jewish marriage is: kedushah and eternity.
Avraham buying the Me'aras HaMachpelah was preparing a home for his continuing marriage, a passageway to Gan Eden where each couple lies side by side.
Rivka's jewelry, like a Jewish home, has a soul: the bracelets radiated Torah and the Luchos.
A person has a fixed allotment of toil and pleasure; he can choose to spend the toil on chesed and be spared it elsewhere.

The Mashgiach explains that the Torah's only two cases of kfitzas haderech are journeys to find a kallah because a shidduch is heavenly, and what is heavenly is not subject to the earthly limits of time and space.
According to the Mashgiach, the bas kol errs about matches not from weakness but because a shidduch is so sublime that even a daughter of prophecy cannot grasp it in this world.
The Mashgiach reads the opening 'lo tov' of the tenth utterance as the voice telling the bas kol 'not this one' after each wrong announcement, until 'matza isha matza tov'.

Citing the Tzemach Tzedek, the Mashgiach explains that the shadchan's lie gives the holy union a slight blemish so it can descend into this world, and reads 'shadchan' as initials of 'sheker dover, kesef notel'.

The Mashgiach measures each holy time by its prohibition of work, which stems from the curse of Adam, and from this shows that women's refraining from work while the Chanukah candles burn reveals their higher kedusha on Chanukah.

The Mashgiach answers his own question on the Chasam Sofer: the women's staying inside and not lighting, for the sake of tznius, is itself the pirsumei nisa, since the miracle of Yehudis was a miracle of tznius.
Bringing the Shinever Rav, the Mashgiach explains that Eliezer could not have known Rivka's size, so the clothing he gave her were samples of the modest dress kept in Avraham's house.
Since Shabbos is pure neshamah, the soul of Knesses Yisrael, a human being can truly be wed to it: soul joins with soul.
The seven days of sheva brachos are the couple's private Shabbos, as the eved ivri has a private shemitah, and their seventh day is a Shabbos of Shabbosos.
Beis Hillel's perutah does not lessen the kallah's dignity: it teaches that the value lies not in what is given but in how, with full awareness of who she is.
The kallah's total passivity at kiddushin, which seems to be not giving, is in fact the highest giving: she gives her very self, not something of herself.
Shabbos, like the kallah, seems only to take, since everything must be prepared for it, yet it is the greatest giver, the source of all brachos for the week.
Being a Jew means surrendering oneself to Hashem, and that is why Jewishness is inherited from the mother, whose nature is to give herself totally.
Shidduchim are where Hashem briefly shows Himself as the One who runs the world, and from that open case one may make a hekesh, an inference, to all the hidden ones.

Cleopatra's question 'what does Hashem do since creation' reflects the view that He made the world like a tape recorder that runs without its maker; the answer 'He makes matches' points to the area where that view visibly fails.
Since Hashem makes the shidduch but will not say a lie, the shadchan's fee is payment for the lie he tells, which explains Rabbi Yaakov Emden's seemingly jesting words.
The lie in a shidduch is the Satan's portion, like the se'ir la'azazel and the goat hairs left sticking out of the tefillin: with the greatest mitzvos he is given something so he will not spoil them.
Eliezer's name is absent from the whole parsha of the shidduch because that shidduch needed no lie and no shadchan; Hashem made it, and Eliezer was only Avraham's messenger.
Eliezer withheld gifts from Besuel because he knew by ruach hakodesh that Besuel would die that night, and did not want to be blamed for poisoning him.
Eliezer's name is withheld precisely in the parsha where he makes the shidduch, because he is the father of all shadchanim and the Torah wants to show that the shadchan does not make the match.
Kiddushin learned from a burial cave is not a bad omen but the best one: the couples of the Me'aras HaMachpela show that the bond of the souls outlives the bodily kiddushin that ends at death.
A shidduch is like Malchus Beis David, which comes from so high a place that even Shmuel HaNavi did not recognize the king; so too the malach does not know the shidduch and must guess.

The tenth maamar opens with 'it is not good' and ends with 'a helper opposite him', mirroring how shidduchim begin with options that are not good before the right one; and it corresponds to 'do not covet', taking one's own and not another's.

The shadchan is paid not for arranging the match, which Hashem does, but for saying the lie that the Satan must be thrown, which explains Rabbi Yaakov Emden's saying that the shadchan takes money for his words.
The seventh day is really the tenth, since three 'days' preceded creation, so Shabbos is Malchus, the tenth; the kallah is Shabbos, which is why the tenth maamar about Chava belonged to Shabbos.

The bar mitzvah is a real chuppah: the boy is wed to the ruach he now receives, and the Zohar's story shows that the shidduch Rabbi Yossi offered supplied the neshamah still missing, making the chassanah complete.

The bar mitzvah boy who counts Sefirah unites both halves of the passuk: the bar mitzvah gives him 'ner mitzvah', and his Sefirah prepares him for 'Torah ohr'; 'seudah shel bar mitzvah' equals 'Torah ohr' in gematria.
A bar mitzvah boy is like the 'mincha chadashah' brought at the end of Sefirah: he presents himself to Hashem at thirteen as a new, pure gift, ready to receive the Torah.

Food, like a person, has a guf and a neshamah: matzah is flour and water, but its neshamah is emunah, and each Yom Tov's food carries that Yom Tov's gift into the one who eats it with the mitzvos connected to it.
Because whatever a person eats becomes part of his body, the Torah puts great emphasis on food; eating at the bar mitzvah seudah means ingesting ner mitzvah v'Torah ohr.
The Mashgiach suggests that the custom of giving bar mitzvah gifts comes from Hashem's words to Dovid on his bar mitzvah, 'ask of Me': our giving to the boy awakens Hashem's giving to him.
He reads 'everything is in the hands of Heaven except fear of Heaven' as a guarantee: since yiras shamayim depends on the person, one who asks for it will surely receive it.
Haman thought Adar, the last month, meant the end of the Jewish people, but for Klal Yisrael time is a circle, and the last month leads them by the hand into Nisan, the first.

A bar mitzvah on the last day of Adar expresses this circle: the last day of the year connects the old year with the new and leads into Nisan, and so the boy is called to continue his forefathers' chain.

The Mashgiach explains the dearness of the Chanukah mitzvah through mesirus nefesh: just as milah was dear to Avraham Avinu because of its pain, what Klal Yisrael gave their lives for in the days of the Chashmona'im became dear to them.

Abolishing Rosh Chodesh would have meant the destruction of Klal Yisrael, since the Yamim Tovim depend on it; this is why Eretz Yisrael was never left without Jews, so the calendar could be set there.
The Greeks did not oppose Torah as wisdom; they opposed Torah as Hashem's heavenly Torah, accepted even where it is not understood, and therefore they targeted milah, which is its precondition.
Wisdom exists among the nations too, but having a portion in Hashem's Torah is only possible through milah.

The fact that printers now issue a separate Sefer Nechemia, against the Gemara, is itself hashgachah: for a generation that has lost confidence, Nechemia's 'remember me for good' becomes the right approach.
Balak's opposition to Klal Yisrael was a struggle to keep the spark of Malchus Beis David captive inside himself, so it should never come out.
Balak himself is the orla over the kedushah of Moshiach, and Pinchas, read right after him, is the mohel: killing Zimri was a milah that removed the klipah from Klal Yisrael.
The Three Weeks are not inherently sad days but the holiest days of Moshiach, covered by an orla of mourning that will be removed and turned into blessing.
Since Hashem acts like a person's shadow, a Jew's mitzvah of milah is as if he were telling Hashem to perform the milah of the whole world.

A bas Levi who remarried on one witness loses maaser because, by not sensing that her husband was alive, she showed she lacks the sensitivity to a bond that defines Shevet Levi, the tribe that sensed Hashem's bond with Klal Yisrael at the eigel.
The mizbe'ach weeps over a divorce because every husband and wife were once together in the earth taken from beneath it, so it testifies that they belong together.

The mizbe'ach measures of the three Batei Mikdash correspond to the relation of Klal Yisrael to its land: twenty-eight for the 'koach' of the first passuk, thirty-two for the 'lev' of a people abroad with their hearts in Eretz Yisrael, and sixty for the shalom of Birkas Kohanim.

Miriam bas Bilgah kicked specifically the mizbe'ach, not the menorah or the Kodesh HaKodashim, because the mizbe'ach testified to the zivug she had betrayed, and a guilty conscience cannot bear its accuser.

Rivkah's birth coinciding with the akeidah is explained by place: the akeidah was on the mekom hamizbe'ach, the source of all zivugim, and as with a zaken mamrei the place itself has power, so there the accusations against Yitzchak's having children were overcome.
Avraham trusted Eliezer with all his wealth without checking him, yet made him swear about Yitzchak's shidduch, showing that a shidduch demands more care than any business.
The Mashgiach applies the Ohr HaChaim's principle of tumah as the residue of departed kedushah to the yoledes: her tumah is a sign of the holy soul she carried, not a flaw in her.

He reads the placement of the milah verse between the boy's and the girl's tumah as the Torah's own answer: the eighth-day light of the bris reaches the mother and cuts off the tumah that should have been longer.
The mikvah is an embassy of the World to Come, of the eighth world where death has no hold, which is why tzaddikim went to the mikvah when their tefillos could not annul a decree.
Since aveilus is separation, the joining of parshiyos in the Sefirah weeks and the Three Weeks is itself the tikkun: like the letters of the Torah, the groups of Jews must be joined.
When the first day of Rosh Chodesh Iyar falls on the thirtieth of Nissan, the Mashgiach sees the month of Nissan going to receive from the 'Rebbe' of Iyar, a model for learning from other groups.
Aveilus is pirud and simcha is yichud: the word chedvah, joy, contains chad, one.
Kayin's sin was not lack of greatness but lack of the point of truth: even in his protest to Hashem he meant himself.

The Rambam is forced to read shalom bayis literally, as avoiding a quarrel over who gets the mitzvah, because he holds that oneg Shabbos is not a Torah obligation from mikra kodesh, so Rashi's reasoning is closed to him.

Since by the Rambam the enactment is for the wife's sake, she can waive it and tell her husband to light his Chanukah light; and a man with no wife would light the Chanukah light, while by Rashi he would still need light to eat by.

Shalom bayis is not a private matter: since the home is a mashal for Hashem and Knesses Yisrael, a husband who yields to his wife arouses Hashem to yield, so to speak, His own interests for the good of Knesses Yisrael.
The Hei at the end of Avraham's 'ohalo' and the reading of Shlomo as 'the King to Whom peace belongs' express the same idea: putting the other's peace before one's own.

Asked why there is no special tefillah for shalom bayis, a gadol answered that there is one, said three times a day: the request that one's soul be like dust, which is the readiness to yield and bear with others.

The Rambam omitted the husband's yielding from the laws of Ishus and placed it in the laws of Chanukah, because on Chanukah Hashem comes into the Jewish home instead of the Jew coming to the Mikdash, showing that He honors Knesses Yisrael more than Himself.

The first parsha says only 'remembrance' because it is about Pesach, when tefillin are not worn; just as 'zichron teruah' refers to a Rosh Hashanah on Shabbos when the shofar is not blown and only remembered.

Since 'totafos' means the four parshiyos, and in the desert the Jews had only the first two, the first parsha could only speak of a remembrance; the second parsha already looks ahead to those born in the desert who would have all four.
Tefillin are the parsha of Yetzias Mitzrayim because both mean entering a new period of attachment to Hashem, and so every bar mitzvah boy goes through his own Yetzias Mitzrayim.
Every mitzvah a Jew does adds to Hashem's tefillin, which speak of the beauty of the Jewish people.
'Or l'arba'ah asar bodkin es hachametz' hints at the boy entering his fourteenth year, when he must search himself for chametz by the light of Torah.
As Klal Yisrael are Hashem's firstborn, the first year after a bar mitzvah is the firstborn of a person's whole life and shapes all that follows.
The Mashgiach reads the derivation of kiddushin from the burial cave not as a bad omen but as its depth: Avraham bought the grave because his bond with Sarah was meant to continue beyond life.
He explains that halachically a marriage ends with life only from the side of the body, while the souls remain united.
He links the bar mitzvah to the kicha-kicha derivation: since the Torah is given as a kallah, receiving the Torah at bar mitzvah is itself a kiddushin.

Through the Chasam Sofer, he shows that Haman could not destroy only the talmidei chachamim, because the Torah is the inheritance of every Jew and lies within him, to come out in his children if not in himself.
He contrasts silver, tied to fire that rises, with Efron's dust, which brings sadness, so that the Machpelah of Torah is acquired with silver and zrizus.
The Mashgiach reads Yaakov's 'kayom', 'as of today', as the heart of his dispute with Esav: the same word 'today' carries two opposite philosophies of life.
He links Esav's 'I am going to die, so what is the birthright to me' with the rasha's 'eat and drink, for tomorrow we die'.
He explains that a bar mitzvah is a wedding in which the boy is the chassan and the holy Torah is the kallah.
He ties Toldos being the sixth sedra to yesod, the foundation of bracha and of tzaddikus, so becoming bar mitzvah in it is a good sign.
Following the Avnei Nezer, a gift the Ribono shel Olam gives the Jews that they do not use is seized by the sitra achra; Achashverosh's feast was the oneg of the Shabbos the Jews failed to keep.
Following the Shem MiShmuel, milah is the source of chiyus and newness, so its neglect let Pharaoh take the "chadash" for himself: "a new king arose".
The Mashgiach reads "kadesh li kol bechor" at the opening of tefillin as the theme of tefillin: a bechor is something that never was before, and tefillin call for that newness each day.
He contrasts weekday tefillin, kabbalas ol malchus shamayim even in darkness, with Shabbos tefillin, which bring chiyus, renewal and kabbalas ol out of love.
The joy of the guests at a bar mitzvah is their own renewal, and this renewal takes back what the new king of Egypt had seized.
The Exodus at Pesach is the Jewish people's bar mitzvah: daas left its exile and the nation came to daas.
A boy does not feel the change at thirteen because the last drop of daas, like the last drop that completes a revi'is, can only be detected with precise instruments.
Shabbos HaGadol is named for the Jewish people becoming 'gedolim', adults, as they came to daas.
The two names of the nasi of Gad, ben De'uel and ben Reuel, point to daas and ratzon, the two ways of becoming bar mitzvah, which the boy should join together.
The custom of bar mitzvah gifts below awakens gifts from Heaven, where a heavenly voice tells the boy he is born today and may ask.
A bar mitzvah in the days before Shavuos fits the season: just as all Jews then become a 'new offering', newborn before Hashem, the boy is reborn as a son of Hashem.
The heavenly call 'You are My son' is placed in the psalm of Gog and Magog because the bar mitzvah boy of a generation that casts off the yoke of Heaven needs it most.
'I will tell of the decree' means making it a fixed law for oneself to repeat, again and again, that one is a child of Hashem.
The minyan for kedushah is learned specifically from the meraglim to show that even ten Jews who are not tzaddikim join into holiness through the good point in each of them.
Combining into one exists only in good; evil has no such joining, so a gathering of Jews draws out what is holy in them.
A twelve-year-old tzaddik still cannot join a minyan, while a bar mitzvah boy can: his entry into the tzibbur, not his personal level, makes the day a public simcha.
The new power of good that the tzibbur receives through the boy is shared with everyone present who rejoices with him and with all of Klal Yisroel.
Parshas Shelach shows two kinds of shluchim, the failed meraglim and the successful Kalev and Pinchas, and every Jew is sent into the world as one or the other.
The 'bride' of the bar mitzvah boy is his new soul, the neshamah yeseirah, which is why the bar mitzvah day can be called his wedding day.
The Mashgiach compares the bar mitzvah soul to the Shabbos soul: both are received as a crown on the head, as recited in Kegavna, that all Jews are crowned with new souls.

It is no accident that the age of thirteen is learned from the passuk calling Shimon and Levi 'brothers of Dinah': at thirteen a boy shows which family he belongs to, and they showed it by defending their sister.
Just as every leaf can be recognized as coming from its tree, a bar mitzvah boy should be recognizable as coming from his family's tree.
The custom in some places to shower the bar mitzvah boy, not only the chosson and kallah, mirrors what happens above, where he is showered with gifts from Heaven.
The Mashgiach reads the tochachah's title 'the words of the covenant' as linking it to bris milah: as the bris removes the covering, so the curses are a covering over blessing.
He matches the seven weeks of consolation to the middos, so that Ki Savo, the sixth, is the week of yesod, the middah of the bris.
He sees in the haftorah's words about the nations, those cut off and those who will serve Klal Yisrael, the two stages of milah and periah.
He notes that the sixth haftorah ends with 've'ameich kulam tzaddikim', tzaddik being the term for yesod, the middah of the week.
Because the blessings are derived from the curses by a hekesh, and what a teacher lacks the student cannot have, the blessings must already be present inside the curses themselves.
The curses of Ki Savo are like an orlah: a covering over great good, and a bris that removes it reveals the hidden blessing.
Elul is the bris milah of the year: Tamuz and Av are the orlah, and in Elul, with the milah and priah, it is revealed that everything was good all along and judgments turn into merits.
The curses at the end of the year in Ki Savo are themselves a bris at the end of the year, matching the bris that completes a child's formation at its end.
The passuk 'umal Hashem' speaks to the generation of Moshiach yet says 'the heart of your children', because a father's teshuvah through the circumcision of the heart takes effect in his child.
A bris is the one mitzvah a father does for his child that is entirely free of ulterior motives, since every Jewish child is circumcised and there is no honor to gain from it.
The Mashgiach links the bris to the season through the passuk of parshas Nitzavim that speaks of Hashem circumcising the heart, which is read in the days of Elul.
He presents Elul as the preparation for Rosh Hashanah, the time that determines the whole year, so that what is done in these days carries weight for the year.
He sees a bris in Elul as made at an auspicious hour, since these are the days when the thirteen middos of rachamim are aroused.

The Mashgiach pairs the ten days of teshuvah with the ten maamaros of creation, so that Yom Kippur matches "lachem yihyeh l'ochlah": the day nature would make the day of eating is the day a Jew rises above it.
He reads the order of night and day in Barchi Nafshi as the order of nature, so that rising at night in these days is itself a step above nature.
Above the sun, beyond nature, is the realm of the thirteen middos of rachamim, which no sin can reach.
Since nature made a man with an orlah, a Jew who cuts it away sets nature aside; therefore milah, on the eighth day, is above nature, as the Maharal says.
The thirteen brisos of milah correspond to the thirteen middos, so a bris in these days receives the thirteen middos that rule at this time.
Citing sefarim, he says the soul of the one whose name is given comes to the naming, and within the first year it is still more connected to this world.
The brachah over the four species goes on the lulav, Yosef the mashpia, rather than the esrog of Dovid and malchus, even though malchus is the theme of every brachah.
Only Yosef among the ushpizin is called 'the tzaddik', a title he earned through his test, and this is the most important of all the middos.

Following the Chasam Sofer, 'there is none greater in this house than I' can be read as Yosef saying that in the 'house' of the Divine Name he is the highest, the lulav, and refusing to lose that rank.
Both orders of the ushpizin are true and both customs exist; by one of them this day belongs to Yosef, so a bris meal in the sukkah today makes Yosef the head of the guests.
The two readings of 'seven and eight', the festival and the bris, are one idea: in both, eight stands beyond the realm of seven.
Seven, the seventy bulls of Sukkos for the nations and the days of creation, is the share given to the world; eight is the Jews' own bond with Hashem, in which the nations have no part.
The meeting of a bris with Shemini Atzeres is not chance but hashgachah pratis, and makes the baby a 'Shemini Atzeres child'.
Yovel, the fiftieth year after seven times seven, carries the same quality of the eighth.
Hashem withheld the promise of the land until Avraham reached Shechem because that is Yosef's place, the place of the bris, and the land is earned through the bris.
Lech Lecha is the parsha of bris milah, and whatever happens in a given week is connected to that week's parsha.
The place where the first galus began, Yosef's sale from Shechem, is exactly where Hashem promised the land, so the start of galus already holds the promise of return.
The Mashgiach reads 'v'charos imo habris' as Hashem holding Avraham's hand, and from this concludes that at every bris Hashem holds the mohel's hand the way a scribe holds his pen.
Since no one can sign in another's name through an agent, the words 'chasam b'os bris kodesh' show that Hashem Himself signs every bris.
Avraham merited Chevron through his bris: the place he bought in Parshas Chayei Sarah is the place of his bris, where Hashem came to him.
The Mashgiach reads the parsha's name, Toldos, as the power and blessing that flow from parents to their children.
He points out that the verses from Yaakov's birth until Avraham's passing are the only ones in the Torah in which all three Avos are alive together.
Three generations at a bris mirror the three Avos together in Toldos, so the parsha's blessings rest on such a family.
Yehuda was not born circumcised precisely because his path is teshuvah: the orlah left for a person to remove is what milah teaches, that man perfects himself.
Grapes and wheat, unlike other fruits, gain a higher blessing when crushed and worked, a sign that being broken can raise a person.
Malki-tzedek, himself born circumcised, could not use milah as proof that one can repair oneself, so he brought bread and wine to console Avraham.
Moshiach ben David embodies teaching teshuvah, and Moshiach ben Yosef the tzaddik who is the foundation of the world.
The Mashgiach reads Chazal's teaching that the angels brought Levi to the Kisei HaKavod to be named as describing his bris, since a name is given at the bris.
Since bris is 612 and milah completes 613, the Mashgiach says it is not only the mitzvah of milah that comes to a bris but the whole Torah.

The Mashgiach links the custom of bentching at a bris with the permission of the kohanim and leviim to shevet Levi's keeping milah in Mitzrayim, which also explains why Levi was named at his bris by Hashem Himself.
He connects Levi, the grandfather of Moshe Rabbeinu, and the passuk 'Torah tziva lanu Moshe' to the child named Moshe at this bris.
Osniel ben Kenaz could restore the forgotten halachos because by conquering Kiryat Sefer he became the owner of the land in which those halachos were written.
Mamre merited that Hashem revealed Himself in his portion because he owned Chevron, the place of milah, which explains Rashi's link between his counsel on the milah and the revelation.
Chevron and Shechem are both places of milah: Chevron, the place of Avraham, the general mitzvah, and Shechem, the place of Yosef, the detail of periah.

The three parts of milah, milah, periah and metzitzah, correspond to what happened in Shechem: the circumcision of its men, the conversion of its women and children, and the war with the surrounding nations drawn from afar.
The greatest kelipos of Eretz Yisroel sit in Chevron and Shechem because these are the places of the holy bris.
The places tied to milah and to the Akeidah had to be bought with money rather than received as a gift, because the bris can only be acquired through mesiras nefesh.
The Mashgiach reads the day's news of an enemy's capture as the visible sign that a heavenly prince of Yishmael has fallen, since kings below fall only when their prince above falls.
The reading of the Nesi'im on Chanukah is explained as breaking the twelve nesi'im of Yishmael, who are twelve angels above.
Yishmael's claim to Eretz Yisroel rests on his milah, but because his milah is empty and without tikkun, his hold on the land is empty too.

Even the preparation for a bris, from the shalom zachar on, is counted as part of the bris, as the poskim show that a father preparing for a bris cannot be called to a din Torah, and so it too helped bring down Yishmael's prince.
The two Harachaman prayers at a bris, for Moshiach and for the kohen tzedek, correspond to Moshe and Eliyahu, the very names of the child.
Rebbe Chaim Meir of Vizhnitz read 'Elokim yechonecha beni' as a blessing that a child born on Chanukah be a true Chanukah child.
A child born on the first day of Chanukah whose bris falls on the last day is bound to Chanukah from birth to bris, and so fits this blessing.
The Mashgiach describes a Chanukah child as a child of dveikus and avodas Hashem.
A bris on Chanukah doubles the revelation of the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, since both the bris and Chanukah reveal them.
The child's name Elisha is itself a sign of healing: if Elisha healed even Naaman, all the more so for Jews.
The kal vachomer in the week's sedra connects to chessed, because kal vachomer, first of the thirteen rules of exegesis, parallels 'Keil', first of the thirteen attributes of mercy.
Yosef's role as sandek for Machir's children was aimed at Gilead specifically, because Gilead was a place under the mazal of bloodshed.
The same mazal of Maadim that can produce a murderer can produce a mohel; Yosef redirected Gilead's nature from killing to milah.
Eliyahu, the angel of the bris, comes from Gilead because of the holiness of the bris that Yosef planted there as sandek.
'Va'eira' can be read as a statement about every generation: Hashem shows Himself to the children too, not only to the Avos, to whoever wants to feel it.
Since Hashem appeared to the Avos with the name Keil Shakai, the name given at Avraham's bris, a bris is a time when Hashem appears even today.
The Mashgiach says the emunah in Hashem's appearing at a bris is greater than seeing it.
Nothing about the timing is chance: a bris in Vaera, where the plagues are healing for Israel, fits the link between refuah and milah on the eighth day.
A passuk whose first and last letters both spell milah is unusual, and it shows that milah carries both chessed for Klal Yisroel and din on the wicked.
In the Megillah, Esther's words that carry Hashem's name in the first letters drew chassadim on Klal Yisroel, while Haman's own words, with the name in the last letters, drew din on the nations.
Milah was given to the Jews as they went down into the exile of Mitzrayim, because exile requires both sides of milah: protection against the nations and the flow of chessed.
Since the main tikkun of Shovevim is on Friday, the sixth day, a bris that falls on a Friday of Shovevim joins the tikkun of milah with the day's own tikkun.
Eating matzah is literally taking geulah into oneself, since what a person eats becomes part of his flesh and blood.
'Bread from heaven' is not only the manna: since the Torah is eternal, every meal a Jew eats is food from Hashem's word rather than from the earth.
The bris seudah lets the participants eat the holiness of the bris into themselves, so refusing it amounts to refusing geulah.
Eliyahu Hanavi is present at every bris, but the degree of his revelation depends on the home and the parents of the child.
The song of Shabbos Shirah, 'Hashem will reign forever', is the song of Moshiach, connecting it with Eliyahu and the bris.
The Mashgiach counts the hardening of the heart itself as a plague on Egypt, harsher than the others.
Since the Torah is a Torah of life, the subject of a parsha is active in the week it is read, so the week of Beshalach is a time to draw strength against hardness of heart.
A bris of the flesh performed in these weeks arouses in Heaven the greater matter of the circumcision of the heart.

The same song at the Sea has a different force on its two reading days: on Shevi'i shel Pesach the time and the reading together bring the lights of redemption, while on Shabbos Shirah the reading alone brings only a semblance.

The choice of haftaros matches the feminine and masculine songs: Shabbos Shirah's haftarah ends with a salvation limited to forty years, while Shevi'i shel Pesach's ends with an eternal salvation for Dovid's offspring.
A bris on the eighth day connects to the eight-stringed harp of the days of Moshiach, so a bris in the week of Shabbos Shirah turns that Shabbos's limited salvation into true lights of redemption.
The 'next day' after Yisro's seudas bris he already added a parsha to the Torah, showing that the bris itself opens a person to Torah.
Hashem takes up the cause of those who fall behind: He fought Amalek for the stragglers outside the clouds, and drew close Yisro, who came late.
Postponing a bris for the child's health reveals how precious a Jew's body is to Hashem, and that very postponement draws down healing for all Jews.
A person cannot know what one mitzvah accomplishes; thousands of Jews may have a salvation through a single mitzvah.
Haman understood that a Jew's real birth is his bris, and he miscalculated only because he did not know Moshe Rabbeinu was born circumcised.
The bris is called a birth because through it the child gains his bond with Torah, mitzvos and the Ribono shel Olam.
Because the days around a birthday share in it, a bris near the day of Moshe Rabbeinu's birth carries a special sign of blessing.
Eliyahu is hidden in the Megillah under the name Charvona and appears exactly at Haman's downfall, because Haman's removal was a bris for the world and Eliyahu is the angel of the bris.
A single bris is not private: it stirs all of creation and removes another piece of the world's orlah, leading toward the revelation of Moshiach.
Joy is linked to milah because milah weakens nature, and true joy comes only when a Jew rises above nature and sees worldly pleasures as fleeting.
Through the miracle of the Megillah it became clear to the Jews that the true 'sasson' is milah and the removal of impurity from the world.
The blessing 'Magen Avraham' refers to Hashem guarding the point of Avraham Avinu inside every Jew, so that it can never be extinguished.
Doing the greatest mitzvah on an infant, without daas or speech, is not a lack but shows that the mitzvah's depth is above daas.
Milah and tefillin, sasson and yikar, stand for two sides of Yiddishkeit: the point above understanding inherited from the Avos, and service with daas.
The 'ad delo yada' of Purim expresses the same point of Avraham Avinu that lies above intellect.

The Mashgiach reads the Chachamim's hesitation as more than a counting rule: a fourth writing of Amalek belongs to the final, complete wiping out of Amalek, and the Megillah's concealment shows that time had not come.
Megillas Esther was given as a spark of Moshiach's light so that Jews can get used to it, since the full light, if it came at once, would be too strong to bear.
Purim will remain when other yomim tovim are nullified precisely because it is not yet finished: its full expression waits for the complete wiping out of Amalek.

Shmuel's view that Esther is not among the holy writings is reconciled: it is one of the twenty-four, but its place is still hidden in heaven until Moshiach comes and the Megillah appears in a new garment.
The Shushan Purim seudah is itself a seudah of bris milah, since the Megillah means removing idolatry from the land, just as the bris removes the orlah.
The many names of chametz all point to a single thing, the yetzer hara, so biur chametz is in essence the removal of the yetzer hara.
The Mashgiach reads milah through Aleinu's words about removing impurity from the land and perfecting the world under the kingship of Hashem.
A bris in Nissan joins two removals, of the orlah and of chametz, and the Mashgiach turns them into a prayer that Hashem remove evil from the whole world.
The Mashgiach sees every bris as a small enactment of the coming of Moshiach, which is why the bris prayers mention Eliyahu and Moshiach.
A bris on the day that was the first day of creation and on a Sunday joins the renewal of the world with the entry of a child into the covenant.
A private simcha of one family is, in the Mashgiach's words, a potential trigger for the Geulah that the whole creation awaits.
Precisely Dan, the lowly tribe that came last, receives a yom tov in which Hashem boasts of its korban, and so too Hashem boasts of the last, lowly generation of galus.
The Mashgiach reads 'this is the korban of Achiezer ben Ammishaddai' as said of the child at the bris: on Dan's day, the child himself is the korban Hashem boasts of.
The generation leaving the final galus will be greater than the generation that left Mitzrayim.
A bris in the days between Shabbos Hagadol and the Seder joins three meetings with Eliyahu Hanavi: the haftarah that announces him, his presence at the bris, and his visit at the Seder.
A bris looks like a private family matter, yet the Mashgiach asks that it act like a spark plug that ignites the general redemption.
Milah is not only a mitzvah that happens to fall before Pesach; it is a precondition of the Korban Pesach, so a bris now is itself a preparation for the Yom Tov.
The severity of kareis on Pesach's mitzvos is read as a sign of their power to connect: what cuts off when missing binds when kept.
Since both Pesach and milah carry kareis and both bind a Jew to Hashem, a bris that falls on Pesach is a bond upon a bond.
Eliyahu Hanavi's presence at both Pesach and the bris, and the good tidings tied to him, make such a bris a time of favor when a person can renew himself and form a new bond with Hashem.
Bris milah is the removal of chametz within a person: what Pesach does to the kelipos in the world, milah does to the orlah.
The four kings Avraham Avinu fought on Pesach are read as the four layers of the orlah, three of the orlah itself and the fourth of the peri'ah, the four kelipos.
Aleinu is said after a bris because it speaks of removing idolatry from the land, which the bris itself models.
The usual blessing that a bris be 'in its time' applies with greater force to a bris on Pesach, since both mitzvos are bonds whose absence brings kareis.
The first letters of the passuk about the festivals of Hashem spell 'my mother' and 'my father', showing that Shabbos and the festivals raise a Jew as parents raise a child.
The Mashgiach ties the bris to the day's word in Lamenatzeach, 'yismechu', reading the count itself as a sign of joy.
The joy of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's companions at Kedoshim shows that a Jew's true joy is in what brings him closer to Hashem.
Going up to Yerushalayim on the festivals lifts each Jew above his tribal root to the shared root of the Avos, since the festivals correspond to the Avos.
The revelation to Avraham after his milah was a revelation of 'seeing', linked through milah to the command that every male appear before Hashem on the festivals.
Like Yerushalayim and the festivals, milah does not belong to any one tribe but to the root above all the tribes.
Because each week of the Omer passes through the Yesod of its middah, Yesod shebeMalchus is the point where all of Yesod has been rectified.
The Mashgiach reads the day of the bris as a siman milsa for the child: a bris in Yesod on the day Yesod is completed points to a child prepared for tzidkus.
He links twins to Matan Torah through the mazal of Sivan, which is te'omim.

The Mashgiach explains Rabbi Yochanan's statement that Eliyahu will expound this parsha: once forbidden foods become kosher at the geulah, the prohibition will remain only for the kohanim, the higher Jews.
Each Jew's letter in the Torah is where his learning becomes bright and his chiddushim come; Emor is where Eliyahu's letter lies, and so it is the parsha he will expound.
The Mashgiach compares the young father, who fought for Yiddishkeit in a time when many strayed, to the bnei Tzadok who kept the charge when Yisrael strayed.
Eliyahu, whom the bris benching calls the kohen tzedek, is both the malach habris and the one whose parsha is Emor, the parsha of the kohanim.
The missing lamed by Naftali shows that a count can have no practical purpose at all and still be worthwhile, because simply coming before Moshe Rabbeinu to be seen and blessed is the purpose.
Eliyahu is the angel of the bris because he himself was moser nefesh, ready to shed his own blood, for the holiness of the bris; so he comes to help a father who sheds his child's blood with joy.
The Mashgiach links the bris to the census: just as the Ramban calls being seen by Moshe a great good, being seen by Eliyahu at a bris is a great good; if one cannot see, one can at least be seen.

Naftali was the last tribe of the last camp, and the last generations before the end of days are its counterpart in time: Bnei Naftali, a 'fallen' generation, yet bound to the first generations through Hashem's help.
Avraham's receiving his name before his milah shows that the essential covenant, a bond of the soul, came first, and the milah was given afterwards as its sign.
The Mishnah in Nedarim, which calls a Jew circumcised even if he is not, proves that the covenant of Klal Yisrael lies in the soul, not the flesh.
Because the first covenant does not depend on milah, a woman shares in it fully, which explains how Rus could take the 'bris milah' upon herself.
The Mashgiach ties the bris to emunah: the covenant means believing in Hashem, like Avraham, the first of the believers.
The name Oved does not just mean one who served Hashem wholeheartedly, since many did; it marks one who had to toil on himself because of the heritage he carried.
The repeated genealogy from Peretz shows that the history to be rectified in Oved began earlier, with Er behind Peretz, and all of it merged into one child.
Because Oved worked so wholly on himself, he could father Yishai, one of those who died without sin, only through the serpent's counsel.
The neighbors, not Rus, named the child because Rus, remembering her origins, held back, and they reassured her that a child with such a history would become an oved.
Every element of the soul has its counterpart in time: the orlah over the bris kodesh corresponds to the covering over the brightest month of the year, and the same avodah removes both.
The Mashgiach reads 'bein hametzarim' as the place where one who seeks the Shechinah can reach it, through toil in Torah and avodah.
Tamuz with its milui equals 'yehi or': the month's letter ches stands for darkness, yet its very name holds the light hidden in it.
Milah is done to an infant precisely because it expresses the root of a Jew that is above daas, like 'ad delo yada' on Purim; it does not depend on his work or understanding.
Milah and tefillin are two opposite holinesses, one above daas and one the peak of daas, and a Jew's path leads from milah to tefillin, from sasson to yekar.
The Mashgiach distinguishes between a bris attended by Eliyahu's emissaries and a special bris that Eliyahu attends in person.
A bris after a family's hard times is, in the Mashgiach's words, all the more precious, not less.
Being present at a bris is itself a merit, a chance to attain great things.
The strength of the kelipah over something is itself a sign of the great kedusha hidden in it: so with the seven nations in Eretz Yisrael and the din over the long summer days of Tammuz.
A parsha named for the wicked Balak is really named for the spark of Moshiach hidden in him, not for Balak the rasha.
The Mashgiach reads Balak's words 'v'hu yoshev mimuli' as his fear that the orlah would be removed and Moshiach revealed, which is why he sent for Bilaam.
A bris held in the week of Balak, just before bein hametzarim, is a symbolic act pointing to Hashem removing the orlah from the world and from these days.
The lifting of the nine days' mourning for a bris is itself a picture of what these days are: their kedusha is covered by an orlah, and the bris removes orlah.
The Mashgiach applies the threefold orlah to the galus: the land is covered by an orlah in place, and the days of mourning by an orlah in time.
A bris in the nine days is a symbolic act: the mitzvah of milah and Eliyahu HaNavi, who comes to every bris, will overcome the orlah of the world, the time and the place.
The Mashgiach reads Rashi's covenant over the fruits in the ark as a definition of a bris: a bris is what keeps a thing from decaying and makes it last forever.
Change and eternity coexist: each generation and moment brings a new task, yet underneath runs one unchanging thread of Klal Yisroel, and the bris is that thread.
A person's name changes with his mission, but what makes him a Jew, his bond to Hashem, does not change at all.
Most mitzvos serve the one who does them, but milah is by its nature a transfer: it hands emunah from one generation to the next.
Because Amalek attacked milah, the mitzvah of continuity, Hashem's war against him is measure for measure 'from generation to generation'.
The Mashgiach reads Moshe Rabbeinu's delay of his son's milah as solidarity with klal Yisroel, parallel to his breaking the luchos rather than remain the one tzaddik apart from the sinners.

Because milah is a sign of belonging to the community, its kareis, like that of eating on Yom Kippur, stems from separation from the klal; so when all Jews ate at the dedication of the Beis HaMikdash, there was no such separation.
The plural 'lamulos' shows that Moshe's act aroused merit above for all the Jews, and once that merit was accepted it was decreed that the redemption from Egypt would begin.
Since Moshe Rabbeinu is connected to Moshiach, the Harachaman for Moshiach mentions his 'chasan damim', and a bris in a generation where milah is weakened is a harbinger of the final geulah.
Because a Jew's thoughts are constantly in Yerushalayim, the Mashgiach says, he is considered as being there all the time, not only on the three festivals.
The Mashgiach applies the Rishonim's answer to the present: a father who must run between doctor and rav to make the bris on time is literally engaged in the mitzvah day and night for all eight days.

He draws a parallel: just as a Jew who longs for Yerushalayim is there all year, a father occupied with the bris for all eight days merits, measure for measure, to see the Shechinah three times a year.
The question why milah is not postponed until the child can understand answers itself: milah belongs to emunah above daas, so it fits precisely the age before daas.
Milah is kept even by Jews far from observance because a person may choose between tzaddik and rasha, but his very Jewishness is above choice and above daas.
Sasson and yekar stand for two poles: milah, wholly without daas, and tefillin, from which one may not divert one's mind, the peak of daas; their coming together is a great preciousness.
Moshe was born circumcised not because he lacked the mitzvah but because, as the redeemer who will remove idolatry from the world, he had to stand outside the orlah from the start, like a mohel.
Following the Maharal, even shevet Levi was never enslaved, since the redeemer came from it and had to come from outside the bondage.
The custom of an early-morning bris is itself a plea that the geulah, which milah stands for, come quickly; a bris pushed to the edge of sunset cries out that the time is already late.
The Mashgiach links this bris to parshas Shemos, where Moshe is born circumcised, and to the start of sefer Shemos, which the Ramban calls the book of geulah.
Dovid's being born circumcised was no chance event: the refinement of his lineage, from Yehudah through Peretz, Nachshon, Boaz and Yishai, left no waste that milah had to remove.
The Mashgiach reads 'michtam' as 'makoso tamah', his wound was whole, and links this temimus to the name Dovid that a child brings into the bris.
A name links a child to the first one who bore it, as a child named Avraham shares in Avraham's yiras shamayim; so a child named Dovid shares in the quality of Dovid.
The Mashgiach reads Yom Kippur itself as a day of milah: the atonement of the day is the circumcision of the heart, rooted in Avraham's bris on that day.

From the Arizal's words about Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair he derives a general rule: doing the mitzvah that defined a tzaddik draws his soul onto the doer, so the father at a bris carries Avraham's soul and its chessed.

He contrasts Amalek, whose scorn for milah earned the erasing of his remembrance, with Israel, whose milah leaves a remembrance, and on this basis explains the custom of naming the child at the milah.

The Mashgiach applies Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen's principle, that a person does not believe in what he has no connection to, to Esav: his other sins could stem from desire, but scorning the birthright exposed that he had no connection to 'reishis'.
He ties together Hashem as the First, the sanctity of firstborns, Israel as Hashem's firstborn and the Torah called 'reishis', so that honoring the bechor is honoring all of them.
He explains that the root of a blemish of the bris is that the first does not go to Hashem, which is why a meal honoring 'reishis' is likened to the eighty-four fasts given for that blemish.
He reads the pidyon haben meal as a reversal of Esav's meal: where Esav ate and drank in scorn of the birthright, Jews eat and drink to honor it.

Following the Chasam Sofer, the Mashgiach reads Haman's 'scattered among the nations' as a halachic claim: a holiness of value among seventy nations is nullified, but Israel's holiness is of the body and is never nullified.
He distinguishes two kinds of redemption: Hashem can redeem Israel's suffering by placing it on the nations, but Israel itself, as 'reishis', can never be exchanged.
He explains Rashi's harsh word for one who says terumah can be redeemed: since Israel is 'reishis', the view that reishis can be redeemed is the view of Bilaam and his students.
Citing the Arizal, he says the firstborn is the reishis through which all the blessing of later children comes, which is why he takes a double portion.
Since the Yerushalmi says Rabbi Menachem never looked at a coin's image at all, even as a child, his holiness was inborn, and so the title 'son of holy ones' credits his parents.
Because his parents were not taken up with money, as people are when making a shidduch, their son was born unable even to look at it.
The Or HaChaim's reason for tumas ohel among Jews, that impurity gathers where great holiness departed, applies in a small way every motza'ei Shabbos when the extra soul leaves.
Rabbi Menachem bar Simai said only one havdalah because, being so holy, he did not need havdalah's protection, only the mitzvah itself.
Pidyon haben is a kind of havdalah: the firstborn must be redeemed because the holiness of the bechor that should have been his has departed, leaving a place that needs protection.
The Torah singles out Esav's despising of the bechorah over his five grave sins because it was a flaw in outlook that reveals who he is, a sign for all generations.
Following Rav Tzadok, not believing in something is a symptom that one has no connection to it, since a person by instinct believes in what he belongs to.

Using a rule of geometry, the Mashgiach argues that whatever has a beginning has an end; Israel, the true reishis, will have a good acharis, while Amalek's lack of a good end shows its reishis is false.
Doing the pidyon haben inside the seudah reverses Esav's feast: he celebrated despising the bechorah, while Jews feast to honor it, and that honor outweighs the mitzvah itself.
Leket, shikchah and peah, the last grain left at the end of the harvest, appear among the festivals of reishis because the last generations are as precious to Hashem as the first fruits.
The aleph-beis expresses the order by which creation runs, so a verse placed after the aleph-beis is complete speaks of something beyond that order.
Both alphabetical chapters of Tehillim close with an extra verse of 'pedus', so redemption itself is the conduct above the order.
Because pidyon is above the order, a pidyon haben in days of strict judgment brings salvation even where the order would not.

The difference between the covenant of Noach and that of milah is that Noach's was in the heavens, a sign to look up at, while milah is in the body, so that a Jew's very physical functions serve Hashem.
'Holech', walking, means the one still on the way is already praised, just as a hava amina that the Gemara rejects is itself Torah learning.
A vine cannot be grafted with another species, and this is the purity and holiness of the Jewish home.
A vine planted indoors keeps its roots in the house while its fruit grows outside, like children rooted in the holiness of the Jewish home who sanctify Hashem's name outside it.
A Jew has a private home and a collective home, the beis knesses, and the collective home is the main one, the source of the private home's contentment.
The nations hate the Jews for the same reason Yosef's brothers hated him: envy, an inner sense that the Jews are nobler and have a future.
Following Rav Shmelke of Nikolsburg, the curse that passersby give no blessing means that a soul reincarnated in food does not merit the brachah of a tzaddik that brings its tikkun.

The command to borrow from the Egyptians belongs inside the warning of makas bechoros because that plague broke Egypt's root of tzaras ayin; the Egyptians' willing giving with chen was itself a result of the plague.
Rashi's two reasons for the donkey's mitzvah map onto its two mitzvos: its help in carrying out the wealth earns redemption, while its likeness to Egypt calls for breaking its neck.

Breaking the neck is for the owner with a begrudging eye: his trait enters the donkey, so it has no kedushah for the Kohen, and destroying it purifies his heart as burning chametz removes the chametz of the heart.
The donkey of Avraham, Moshe and Moshiach was created at twilight on Erev Shabbos, a time of haste, so it joins the donkey's simplicity with the zrizus of matzah and lacks the donkey's laziness.
The lack of great attainments in the last generation is itself what fits it to bring Moshiach: the simpler the emunah, the more strength it gives Moshiach's simple donkey.
At the Akeidah Avraham's levels and sense of Hashem were taken from him, lowering him to the state of the generation before Moshiach, and he went forward on the donkey with simple emunah.
